name: Emeka Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew building new power lines, setting towers and pulling conductor with a tension machine. My two-year technical diploma helps with the drawings, but my eye is on the twelve people around the crane. A line finished without an injury is a good day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hotel nights away from home. My wife Grace runs a catering business, and our grown children visit when they can, so I would rather be at our own table. I use an AI drafting tool now and then, after it has shown it can save time, but I check every fitting myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can keep its small shortcuts if it leaves the construction crew good drawings. The crane still has to set the tower and someone still has to check the tension on the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace and I have the house paid and more than six months saved. My crew chief wage is good, her catering orders are steady, and there are other line contractors nearby if I ever need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading tower builds and use the drafting tool I already open now and then for the weekly materials list. I would keep the same household budget and visit Grace at home on my days off instead of buying another gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The hotel weeks still tire me, but there is no new money worry in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the tool get wrong on a materials list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong clamp on a tower drawing can waste a whole morning. I caught the wrong size before anyone loaded the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the road work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I still like seeing a completed line cross the fields, and Grace and I have not settled the exact retirement date.

say: I would accept small **office shortcuts** while insisting crews receive checked construction drawings.
I would tell friends that **tower erection** still needs cranes, skilled hands and careful wire tension.
think: Our **paid house**, savings and two incomes make present work feel secure.
The **hotel weeks** are tiring, yet the plateau adds no income threat.
do: Keep leading **tower builds** and checking clamps against drawings.
Continue using the existing **materials-list tool** only for rough drafts.
feel: **Calm** about money, with ordinary fatigue from travel.
S0.quote: A wrong clamp on a tower drawing can waste a whole morning.
fieldNote: He has higher pay, a second income, substantial assets and **many nearby contractors**.
His occasional AI drafting is an **existing habit** and still receives a hands-on drawing check.

steps.text: Keep leading tower builds and checking materials against drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that faster buying and booking could help, but the people who hang the wire should check the plan. I would ask the company to test the new system on one build before changing every site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office jobs may shrink. I think my own construction hours will hold, although a faster supply chain could mean fewer hotel nights and less travel pay; Grace’s catering work is separate and still has customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI ordering screen if the one-build trial catches missing fittings. I would compare its first order with the tower drawings and ask a storekeeper to show me the error log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about what lower travel pay could leave us after road costs, but not frightened for the house. Grace and I have enough put by to adjust if those allowances shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the hotel allowance matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays for the road meals and some of the family visits I miss. If it falls with fewer nights away, some costs fall too, so I would compare the net pay before changing our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why require a trial before learning the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have watched a tidy order arrive with the wrong steel. Show me a real tower build that works, then I will learn the AI ordering screen.

say: I would ask for a **one-build trial** before AI ordering becomes standard on tower sites.
I would keep **crew checks** on fittings and drawings even if buying moves faster.
think: My **construction hours** seem safe, though travel pay could change with fewer hotel nights.
Grace’s **catering income** and our savings protect the household if allowances fall.
do: Learn the new **AI ordering screen** if a real build trial catches missing fittings.
Compare the first **tower order** with drawings and the storekeeper’s error log.
feel: **Anxious** about changing travel pay while core household income stays sound.
S1.quote: Show me a real tower build that works, then I will learn the AI ordering screen.
fieldNote: His steady adaptability depends on **proof from a build**, not a sales promise.
He distinguishes reduced gross travel pay from possible **lower road costs**, so no spending cut is claimed.

steps.text: Learn new AI ordering controls after a successful one-build trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 can make the drawings but cannot string conductor between towers. Around 2031 robots may do that work, and a live construction site is where they must prove themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to still be working when those robots arrive unless Grace and I choose a different date. A reduced crew could cut my hours, but the paid house, savings and nearby contractors give me room to seek another post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company for a written 2031 crew plan and keep building lines in the meantime. If two rosters show fewer paid days, I would apply to nearby contractors, leaving only for a posted role with comparable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours because the timing lands before I have settled retirement. I am not trapped, but I would hate to see good apprentices sent home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a comparable offer need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough paid days to replace my present wage after travel costs. I would ask for the roster in writing before leaving a crew I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as a robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would check the accounts with Grace and stop only if we can cover the years ahead. The machine date is not a retirement fund.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** changes drawings before capable robots can string lines around 2031.
I would demand a **site trial** before tower crews are reduced.
think: The **2031 robot date** may arrive while I still need my crew chief wage.
Our **assets and local contractors** offer choices if a reduced crew cuts paid days.
do: Keep **tower construction** shifts while the company offers them.
Apply to **nearby contractors** after two reduced rosters, leaving only for a posted comparable-pay role.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic hours loss, with money and local options giving control.
S2.quote: The machine date is not a retirement fund.
fieldNote: He considers a job search only after **two reduced rosters**.
A move requires a posted role with **comparable net pay**, and retirement remains tied to household accounts.

steps.text: Keep taking company tower builds while paid shifts continue
Apply nearby after two reduced rosters; leave only for a posted comparable-pay role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is enough to test a machine on a tower site in rain and crosswind. A safe lift must be boring every time, not impressive once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may handle the drawings and ordering, while hands-on robots arrive around 2034. I may have finished regular site work by then if Grace and I find our retirement numbers sound, but I cannot promise it today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew through this first year and show the younger foreman how I check a tension machine. I would review the household accounts with Grace each winter, then decide when regular travel can end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about next year’s wages. The longer run gives me time to finish a line and hand over the judgement that is hard to write down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would let you stop travelling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The amount is not set yet. We would need the house, daily costs and Grace’s catering income covered without my hotel work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a trial role after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it were a paid role with a proper schedule and Grace and I wanted the travel. I would not treat a possible vacancy as money in our plan.

say: I would demand **crosswind trials** before 2034 robots handle tower construction.
I would teach the next **foreman** to check wire tension by the machine and the site.
think: I may leave regular travel before **2034**, conditional on accounts and Grace’s income.
The **2031 desk changes** touch drawings more than my hands-on construction work.
do: Keep leading **tower sites** this year and teach the younger foreman tension checks.
Review **retirement accounts** with Grace each winter before settling a travel exit.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, with interest in a careful handover.
S3.quote: A safe lift must be boring every time, not impressive once.
fieldNote: He expects a possible exit before robots, but names **no fixed date**.
Any later trial role requires a clear **paid schedule**, rather than an assumed offer without hours.

steps.text: Keep leading tower builds this year and teaching the younger foreman tension checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices a decade gives them time to learn the trade properly before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. The company still owes them real site hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our health and accounts hold, I expect Grace and I to have ended my regular tower travel before 2036. I would be sixty eight then, and a robot arriving in 2039 should not decide what we can afford now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present tower rota during 2026 and record two careful lifts for the apprentices to study. In the first year after 2036, if I am retired as planned, I would stay out of crew scheduling and check our household budget with Grace; if I am still employed, I would work only the shifts offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long view. I want the next crew to know why we stop a lift, not merely which button stops it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Grace and I will choose the date from our savings, her catering income and our health. The scenario gives me more time, not a reason to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do apprentices learn from a stopped lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A swinging conductor can pull a fitting sideways before the meter shows trouble. I make them watch the crew on the ground as well as the gauge.

say: I would press for **real site hours** for apprentices before thinking AI and later robots reshape construction.
I would tell the crew that **safe lifts** require judgement beyond a button.
think: I expect to end regular tower travel before **2036** if health, savings and Grace’s income allow.
The **2039 robots** are too late to threaten my present wages on that plan.
do: Keep the **2026 tower rota** and record two safe lifts for apprentices.
Review the **household budget** with Grace after 2036 if retired as planned.
feel: **Calm** about income, committed to passing on site judgement.
S4.quote: I want the next crew to know why we stop a lift, not merely which button stops it.
fieldNote: His 2026 crew work is explicit, while **post-2036 employment** remains conditional.
The planned retirement rests on **health and household accounts**, with no early exit claimed.

steps.text: Keep the 2026 tower rota and record two safe lifts for apprentices
Work only offered tower shifts after 2036 if still employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach tower construction in 2031 before Grace and I settle my retirement date. A written crew plan, proper site trials and posted local jobs with comparable pay would give me real choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the apprentice gets enough paid site hours to learn a safe lift. A certificate cannot feel a conductor swinging beside the tower.

headlineQuote: A certificate cannot feel a conductor swinging beside the tower.
portrait: **Emeka**, 58, is a highly skilled tower-construction chief with a technical diploma, higher pay and more than six months saved.
Grace’s **catering income**, their paid home and plentiful nearby jobs give the household several options.
He uses **AI occasionally** after a proven trial and favours apprenticeships, crew judgement and paid work over uncertain promises.
The **2028 case** worries him because robots could reach his field work before his retirement date is settled.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce paid tower shifts around 2031 before he chooses a retirement date.
whatWouldHelp: A written **crew plan**, site trials and posted comparable-pay roles would give him choices.
